Ice covered region - Polar region - Sparsely populated.
The polar lands are covered with ice through the year, so no crop can be grown and almost nobody lives there.

Administrative city - Capital of the country - Tokyo.
An administrative city is the seat of government, usually the capital, and Tokyo is the capital of Japan.

Shifting agriculture - Small size of farm - Harmful farming.
Only a tiny patch can be cleared and burnt by hand, and because the forest is destroyed and the soil left exhausted and eroded, the practice is harmful.

Cottage industry - Use of manpower - Weavers.
A cottage industry is carried on at home with hand tools and family labour, and handloom weaving is the standard example.

Global Positioning System (GPS) - Artificial satellite - Communication.
GPS fixes a position on the earth by receiving signals from a group of artificial satellites, and those satellites are a means of communication.

(C) Birth rate.
Population changes through births, deaths and migration. Literacy, sex ratio and age composition describe the composition of a population, not the change in its size.

(D) Forests.
In a village the land is under crops, pasture, forest, farm ponds and houses. Industry, trade and recreation are urban land uses.

(B) Monoculture, use of machineries, temperate region, cereal production.
Extensive commercial grain farming is practised on very large temperate farms with machinery and a very small labour force, and it raises a single cereal, chiefly wheat, for sale.

(A) Iron and steel industries.
Iron and steel is made from iron ore, coal and limestone, all minerals. Textiles, sugar and food processing use farm produce, so they are agro-based.

(B) Transportation of goods.
Carrying goods is a service, so it is tertiary. Agriculture and honey production are primary and petrochemicals is a secondary activity.

True.
A large working age group means more earners for every dependant, more output and more saving, so the possibility of economic development is high. This advantage is called the demographic dividend.

False.
Tertiary occupations produce no goods, but they are productive all the same. Transport, trade, banking, teaching and medicine add value and make production and exchange possible at all.

False.
The Kalahari is the home of the Bushmen. The Eskimos, or Inuit, live in the Arctic lands of North America and Greenland.

True.
There is no single world definition. Each country fixes its own, differing in the minimum age and in whether reading alone, or reading and writing, or arithmetic as well, is required. In India a person aged seven and above who can read and write with understanding is counted literate.

False.
Where people settle is decided first of all by relief, water supply, soil, climate and the availability of building material. Physical factors control the site and the situation of every settlement.

(D) Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A broad base does show many children and a broad apex does show many elderly, so both statements are true. But the apex tells us about the old, which cannot explain what the base tells us about the young, so R does not explain A.

(b) Lakes.
Plains, plateaus and mountains are landforms, that is parts of the relief of the land. A lake is a waterbody, so it is the incorrect factor.

Ascending order of population:
(b) Suburb - (c) City - (a) Metropolitan city - (d) Megacity.

Group (b) - Social Geography, Political Geography, Economic Geography, Soil Geography.
All four are branches of geography. Group (a) mixes the umbrella term Social Science with three separate subjects, and groups (c) and (d) each mix subjects that belong to different disciplines.

Ascending order of capital investment:
(d) Micro scale industries - (b) Small scale industries - (a) Medium scale industries - (c) Large scale industries.

Moderate temperature with reliable rainfall allows crops to be grown and life to be comfortable, so monsoon Asia and Western Europe are densely peopled. Extreme cold in the polar lands, extreme dryness in the deserts and the hot wet equatorial forest with its leached soil and disease all make settlement difficult, so those areas are nearly empty. Climate therefore controls the distribution of population.

A literate person can take up skilled and better paid work, use new methods and know his rights, and literate parents look after health, nutrition and family size better. Literacy and the social and economic condition of a country therefore rise and fall together, which is why the literacy rate is used as an indicator of development.

The Chota Nagpur plateau is made of ancient hard rocks that are exceptionally rich in coal, iron ore, mica, bauxite and copper, and the minerals lie close to the surface so they can be worked open cast. Cheap labour is available, railways link the area to Kolkata and to the iron and steel plants nearby, and those plants provide a ready market. Hence mining has developed there.

The physiography of a region decides how much of it is usable at all. Level land can be farmed, built on and crossed by roads and railways; rivers give water and power; and the rocks decide what minerals are available. Rugged mountains, deserts and marsh allow none of this. Since every other factor must work within these limits, regional development depends on physiography.

Geography now studies new problems - population growth, urbanisation, pollution, climate change, disaster management and regional planning - and it has gained new tools in remote sensing, GIS and GPS. As the subject takes in each new problem and each new technique, and as it works with more and more other disciplines, its scope keeps widening.

Extensive agriculture is carried on over very large holdings with machinery and a small labour force, and a single crop is grown. The family cannot consume such a large output, so the whole produce is sold in the market for profit. That is why it is a commercial type of agriculture.

Lumbering in equatorial forests: the forest is evergreen and mixed, with hundreds of species standing scattered among each other, so a wanted tree is hard to find; the wood is hard and heavy and does not float; there is dense undergrowth, heat, rain and disease, and few routes. So lumbering here is small in scale and mostly for local use.
Lumbering in temperate forests: the coniferous forest is a pure stand of one softwood species, the trees are tall and straight with little undergrowth; the wood is light and floats down the rivers; the frozen winter surface helps in dragging logs; and there is heavy demand for timber and pulp. So lumbering here is highly commercial and mechanised.

Stage 1, high stationary: both the birth rate and the death rate are very high, because of poverty, disease, famine and no medical care, so the two cancel each other and the population is nearly stationary. Life expectancy is low and the population is young.
Stage 5, declining: both rates are low, but the birth rate has fallen BELOW the death rate because families are very small and the population has aged, so the total population declines. Life expectancy is high and the proportion of elderly is large, as in Japan, Germany and Russia.

Waterways: the cheapest means for heavy and bulky goods; very slow; no track has to be built, only ports; limited to coasts, rivers and canals.
Airways: the fastest means and the costliest; carries light, valuable or urgent goods and passengers; needs airports and skilled staff; can cross mountains, deserts and oceans that other means cannot.

Physical region: defined by a natural feature such as relief, climate, soil or vegetation, as in the Himalayan region or the Thar desert; its boundary is natural and changes only over a very long time.
Political region: defined by administration, as in a state, a district or a country; its boundary is drawn by people and can be changed by a decision, as when a new state is formed.

Determinism: the view that the physical environment decides human activity, and that people can do only what nature permits. Its supporters, such as Ratzel and Semple, held that climate and relief shape a people's occupations, character and history.
Possibilism: the view that nature offers a range of possibilities and that people choose among them according to their culture and technology. Its supporters, such as Vidal de la Blache, pointed to irrigated deserts, reclaimed land in the Netherlands and settlement in the Arctic as proof that man is an active agent, not a passive one.

In a village most of the land is under farming, because farming is the chief occupation.
Crop land takes the largest share, and is further divided into irrigated and unirrigated, and into net sown area and area sown more than once.
Pasture and grazing land supports the cattle.
Forest and wasteland lie on the outskirts.
Fallow land, current and old, is left to recover its fertility.
Land put to non-agricultural use carries the houses, the threshing floor, the cattle sheds, the village tank, the temple, the school and the field paths.
So rural land use is decided almost entirely by the needs of agriculture, and the built up area is small.

Fishing depends on a combination of physical and human factors.
A broad continental shelf, where the sea is shallow and sunlight reaches the bed, so that plankton can grow.
The meeting of a warm and a cold current, which stirs up nutrients and multiplies the plankton on which fish feed, as off Newfoundland and Japan.
A broken, indented coastline, which gives natural harbours and shelter for boats.
A cool climate, which helps to preserve the catch.
A hinterland of forest and hills, which gives timber for boats and leaves farming difficult, so that people turn to the sea.
And on the human side: skilled fishermen, boats, nets and refrigeration, cold storage and quick transport, a large market, and capital and government support.
The great fishing grounds of the world - the North-West and North-East Atlantic and the North-West Pacific - have all of these together.

An artificial satellite is a man-made body put into orbit round the earth, and a communication satellite receives a signal from one point and sends it on to another.
Its importance: it carries telephone, television, radio and internet signals across oceans and over mountains without any cable; it gives instant contact between any two places on earth; it carries weather pictures and cyclone warnings that save life; it makes tele-education and telemedicine possible in remote villages; it supports GPS and navigation; it is used in survey, mapping and resource exploration through remote sensing; and it is essential in disaster management and defence.
INSAT and GSAT in India are examples.

Regional imbalance means that some regions of India develop far faster than others.
Its causes are: an unfavourable physical setting, such as rugged relief in the hills, drought in the rain shadow and poor soil in the plateau; the uneven distribution of minerals and water; poor transport and power supply in the interior; low literacy, poor health and low skills; the concentration of industry and investment in a few already developed regions, because investors go where infrastructure already exists; the neglect of the interior under colonial rule, when development followed the ports; and political and administrative neglect since.
The result is that people, industry and income concentrate in a few regions while others lose their young people to migration and fall further behind.

Geography studies the earth as the home of people, and explains why one place differs from another.
Its nature is dualistic, because it studies the physical environment and human activity together and is both a natural and a social science.
It is spatial, since it always asks where a thing is and why it is there.
It is integrating, since it draws on geology, economics, sociology, history and other subjects.
It is dynamic, since the earth and human activity both keep changing.
And it works at every scale, from a village to the whole world.

Human factors are those created by people themselves. They can gather population into a place the physical setting would not favour, and empty a place that it does.
Economic activity is the strongest of them. Wherever industry, mining, trade or plantation work offers wages, people gather. The Ruhr in Germany, the Damodar valley in India and Kimberley in South Africa are crowded because of coal, iron and diamonds, not because of their relief or climate.
Transport and communication decide whether a place can be reached and its produce sold. Population is dense along river valleys, coasts, railway lines and highways, and thin where there are no routes, as in the interior of the Amazon basin.
Urbanisation draws people continuously from village to town, because the town concentrates work, education, medical care and entertainment. Mumbai, Delhi, Tokyo and New York have grown in this way.
Political factors matter greatly. Peace, law and order and a settled government attract people and investment, while war and persecution empty a region, as in Syria. Government policy can create population where there was none, as Brazil did by building Brasilia and India by building Chandigarh.
Social and cultural factors work the same way. Religious centres such as Varanasi and Mecca hold large populations, and so do educational centres such as Pune and Oxford.
Technology allows people to live where they could not before, by irrigating deserts as in Israel and Rajasthan, by air conditioning, and by reclaiming land from the sea as in the Netherlands.
So the physical setting decides where people CAN live, and the human factors decide where they actually DO live.

By the source of their raw material industries are classified into four groups.
Agro-based industries use the produce of farming. Because farm produce is bulky and often perishable, these industries are located in the growing area itself. Examples: sugar, cotton textiles, jute, edible oil, tea processing, tobacco and food canning.
Mineral based industries use minerals dug out of the earth. Minerals are heavy and lose weight in processing, so these industries are located near the mine, the coal field or a port. Examples: iron and steel, cement, aluminium, petrochemicals and heavy chemicals. They need large capital, much power and water, and they are the basic industries on which other industries depend.
Pastoral or animal based industries use the produce of animals reared by man. Examples: dairy and milk processing, butter and cheese, leather and footwear, woollen textiles, meat packing and bone meal. They are located near the grazing region or near the market, since milk and meat are perishable.
Forest based industries use the produce of forests. Examples: paper and pulp, plywood and hardboard, furniture, matches, rayon, lac, resin and turpentine. They are located near the forest, because timber is heavy and costly to move.
A fifth, marine based group is sometimes added for industries that use the produce of the sea, such as fish canning, fish oil and sea food processing.
The classification is useful because it explains WHERE an industry will be found: an industry whose raw material is heavy, bulky or perishable goes to the raw material, while one whose raw material is light goes to the market.
